titleText.es: Puedes mirar a cualquier parte de prácticamente cualquier cosa hecha por el hombre y pensar:
titleText.en: You can look at any part of practically anything made by humans and think:
titleText.noteEn: The archived Spanish title text ends at the colon; the original English title text continues with the thought that some engineer was frustrated while designing it.

regions.labelEs: ESTE SEMÁFORO SIEMPRE DURA UNA ETERNIDAD. ME GUSTARÍA ATIZAR AL IMBÉCIL QUE DISEÑÓ ESTE CRUCE.

applications.explanationEn: Me identifies the person with the wish, gustaría makes it polite and conditional, and atizar stays in its dictionary form as the desired action.
Gustaría keeps the full stem gustar and adds -ía, the conditional ending used here in a polite wish.
Al combines a and el; the a marks the specific person directly affected by the proposed action.
Quién carries an accent because it directly asks for a person's identity.

regions.labelEs: TIENE RAZÓN. ¡DEBERÍA HABER ACORTADO EL SEMÁFORO! NO IMPORTAN LAS HORAS DE SIMULACIÓN Y PRUEBAS QUE LLEVÉ A CABO. NO IMPORTA QUE ESTE CRUCE INTERACTÚE CON SUS VECINOS DE FORMAS COMPLICADAS Y QUE ME LLEVARA UNA SEMANA CONSEGUIR UNA SECUENCIA DE TIEMPOS QUE EVITARA ATASCOS BRUTALES.

applications.explanationEn: Tiene is the form of tener used for formal usted here, and razón completes the expression for acknowledging that person as right.
Debería keeps the whole verb deber and adds -ía, the conditional ending used in this past-looking criticism.
Debería supplies “should,” haber supplies “have,” and acortado is acortar's completed-action form.
No negates importar, and the plural form importan agrees with the later plural subject horas.
Llevé changes for the speaker and completed past time, while a cabo remains the fixed completion phrase.
No importa treats the following situation as the single thing being dismissed, so importar remains singular.

applications.exampleEs: NO IMPORTA QUE ESTE CRUCE INTERACTÚE
applications.explanationEn: No importa que frames the interaction as the situation being dismissed, so interactúe uses the special present subjunctive form.
The second que continues the same no importa frame, and llevara uses the past-looking subjunctive form for the time that was required.
Me identifies whose time was used, llevara supplies the time-taking verb, una semana gives the duration, and conseguir stays in its dictionary form for the activity.

applications.exampleEs: UNA SECUENCIA DE TIEMPOS QUE EVITARA
applications.explanationEn: Una secuencia introduces the sought, not-yet-identified thing; que then introduces evitara in the special form used for the result that desired sequence needed to achieve.

regions.labelEs: ESTÁ CLARO QUE SOY UNA BASURA DE INGENIERO Y QUE USTED TIENE UNA SOLUCIÓN MEJOR. ADELANTE, MUÉSTREME SU SECUENCIA PROPUESTA.

applications.explanationEn: Soy changes for the speaker, while una basura de frames ingeniero as the role in which the speaker sarcastically claims to be terrible.
Muestre is mostrar's formal usted command, and me is attached to identify the speaker as the person who should be shown it.

regions.labelEs: BÁJATE DE MI MALDITO CAPÓ ANTES DE QUE ARRANQUE Y TE LANCE CONTRA EL TRÁFICO.

applications.explanationEn: Baja is the positive informal command of bajar, and the attached te marks the listener in the pronominal verb bajarse.
Bájate addresses one informal listener and de introduces the surface that person is ordered to leave.

applications.exampleEs: ANTES DE QUE ARRANQUE Y TE LANCE
applications.explanationEn: Antes de que introduces two still-pending actions; arranque and lance both use the special subjunctive forms triggered by that connector.

regions.labelEs: NO PUEDE. LA LUZ ESTÁ EN ROJO.

applications.explanationEn: Cuándo carries an accent because it directly asks at what time the change will occur.
Cambiará keeps the full verb cambiar and adds -á for the future of one thing.
El marks one particular Tuesday; Spanish uses the article directly where English normally uses “on.”

cards.noteEn: Dura is a form of durar, which describes how long something continues. It is unrelated to dura meaning “hard” when used as an adjective.
Una eternidad often exaggerates how long something feels rather than literally claiming that it never ends.

example.en: The wait felt like an eternity.

cards.questionEn: How do you politely say that someone would like to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use me, te, le, nos, os, or les for the person, then gustaría, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The short word identifies who has the wish: me gustaría means “I would like,” te gustaría means “you would like,” os gustaría means “you all would like” in Spain, and le gustaría can mean “he, she, or formal you would like.” Gustaría stays singular because the following activity is treated as the thing that would be pleasing.

example.en: I would like to learn Italian.

cards.noteEn: Gustaría is gustar with the ending -ía. With a short word such as me, te, or le, it politely says who would like something: me gustaría means “I would like.”

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.
Atizar is informal when it means striking someone or something.

cards.answerEn: a + el before a specific person; often “the” or “to the” in English
cards.noteEn: Spanish contracts a + el to al. The personal a can mark a specific person who receives or is affected by an action; English may use “the,” “to the,” or no separate preposition, depending on the verb.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.
Imbécil is a direct insult and can sound harsh. It is not a neutral description of a person.
Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: he or she designed; formal you designed
cards.noteEn: The final accented -ó marks a completed past action by one person. Context identifies whether the subject is he, she, or formal you.
For roads, cruce is the place where routes cross.

example.es: Gira a la derecha en el cruce.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.answerEn: on earth; the hell (informal question emphasis)

cards.noteEn: The final accented -é marks a completed past action by the speaker.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is right?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of tener followed by razón.
cards.noteEn: Spanish describes someone as “having reason” rather than using ser with a word for “right.” Tener changes for the person and time: tengo razón means “I am right,” and tienes razón means “you are right.” Razón stays unchanged.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone should have done something?
cards.answerEn: Use debería, or the matching form such as deberías, then haber, then the action's completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: The completed-action form, often called a past participle, commonly ends in -ado for -ar verbs and -ido for -er or -ir verbs: llamar becomes llamado and comer becomes comido. Haber and that final form stay unchanged; debería changes for the person, as in deberías for informal “you.” This pattern often expresses regret or criticism about a past action.

After a verb such as debería, haber remains in its dictionary form and combines with a completed-action form such as llamado or comido. In this construction, haber is a helper rather than the hay construction meaning “there is.”
Acortado is the completed-action form of acortar, “to shorten.” Regular -ar verbs replace -ar with -ado to make this form.

cards.answerEn: Neighboring traffic lights can be timed as one network so that vehicle flows reach each intersection at manageable moments.
cards.noteEn: Traffic engineers model arrival patterns and queue lengths when choosing signal timings. Shortening one red phase in isolation can send traffic into a downstream queue or block another movement, so a locally shorter wait can produce worse network-wide congestion.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something does not matter, or dismiss it with “never mind”?
cards.answerEn: Put no before importa for one thing or a whole situation, and before importan for plural things.
cards.noteEn: The thing that does not matter controls the verb: no importa el precio uses singular importa, while no importan los detalles uses plural importan. A following clause normally begins with que. Tone and context decide whether English uses “it doesn't matter” or “never mind.”
Importan is plural because the things that matter are plural. Compare importa el detalle, “the detail matters,” with importan los detalles, “the details matter.”

cards.answerEn: I carried out; I conducted (as part of llevar a cabo)
cards.noteEn: Llevé is the completed past form for the speaker. In llevar a cabo, llevar does not mean physically carrying something; the whole expression means completing or conducting an activity.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone carries out or conducts a plan, test, or activity?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of llevar followed by the fixed words a cabo.
cards.noteEn: Only llevar changes for the person and time. A cabo remains fixed, and the activity being conducted follows afterward. The expression is not about physically carrying an object.

example.es: El laboratorio llevó a cabo dos pruebas.
example.en: The laboratory carried out two tests.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of llevar a cabo (“to carry out”)
cards.noteEn: This a is a required middle piece of the fixed expression llevar a cabo. Translate the three-word expression together.

example.es: Vamos a llevar a cabo una revisión.
example.en: We are going to carry out a review.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes llevar a cabo (“to carry out”)
cards.noteEn: Cabo has several meanings on its own, but after llevar a it completes the fixed expression for conducting or completing something.

example.es: El equipo llevó a cabo el plan.
example.en: The team carried out the plan.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that a situation does not matter?
cards.answerEn: Use no importa que, then put the situation's verb in the subjunctive form.
cards.noteEn: No importa presents a reaction to the situation rather than asserting that situation as the main point. Que introduces it, and the following verb takes a special form called the subjunctive. A present-looking -ar verb normally changes to an e ending, as in interactuar → interactúe; a past-looking event can use an -ara or -iera form, as in llevar → llevara.

example.en: It does not matter if you arrive late.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.noteEn: Interactúe is a special form of interactuar used when the interaction is presented under a reaction, judgment, wish, or other non-statement frame rather than asserted on its own.

example.es: No importa que interactúe con otros sistemas.
example.en: It does not matter that it interacts with other systems.

cards.noteEn: Sus agrees with the plural things owned, not with the owner. The same Spanish form can also mean “his,” “her,” or “their” in other contexts, so context identifies the owner.
Vecinos can describe nearby people or nearby things of the same kind.

example.es: Los pueblos vecinos comparten una carretera.
example.en: The neighboring towns share a road.

cards.answerEn: in (as part of de forma, in a … way)

cards.noteEn: In de formas followed by a description, formas means ways or manners of doing something.
The ending -as matches a feminine plural noun such as formas.

cards.questionEn: How do you say how long an activity takes someone?
cards.answerEn: Use a short word for the person, a form of llevar, the duration, and then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Me, te, le, nos, os, or les identifies the person whose time is used; os is the form for informal plural “you” in Spain. Llevar changes for the time being described, while the final action remains in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form. In this construction, llevar means “to take time,” not “to carry.”

example.en: It took me two hours to finish.

cards.answerEn: it took; it would take (in a past subjunctive form)
cards.noteEn: Llevara is a past subjunctive form of llevar. In the time-taking construction, it describes the amount of time an activity required rather than carrying an object.

example.es: Dudaba que me llevara tanto tiempo.
example.en: I doubted that it would take me so long.

cards.answerEn: to obtain; to work out; to achieve
cards.noteEn: Conseguir can mean obtaining a result through effort, not only physically getting an object.

example.en: We want to reach an agreement.

cards.answerEn: Use the subjunctive after que when describing that unknown person or thing.
cards.noteEn: Spanish treats a known person differently from one you are still trying to find. Conozco a alguien que habla inglés means “I know someone who speaks English.” Busco a alguien que hable inglés uses hable because no particular person has been identified.
cards.questionEn: Which verb form do you use when you are looking for a person or thing that has not been identified—and may not exist?

example.es: Busco a alguien que hable inglés.
example.en: I am looking for someone who speaks English.

cards.noteEn: Tiempos can mean deliberately chosen timings, not only time in a general sense.

example.es: Ajustaron los tiempos de las señales.

cards.noteEn: Evitara is a past subjunctive form of evitar. It can describe a desired or not-yet-identified thing by the result it was supposed to achieve.

example.es: Buscaban una ruta que evitara el centro.
example.en: They were looking for a route that would avoid downtown.

cards.noteEn: Brutal can intensify something as extreme or severe; it need not describe physical violence.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish harshly say that someone is terrible at a role?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of ser, then una basura de, then the role.
cards.noteEn: Basura literally means “trash,” so this is insulting or self-deprecating rather than neutral. Una basura stays feminine because basura is a feminine noun, regardless of the person's gender; only ser changes for the person and time.

cards.answerEn: terrible; rubbish; worthless (in an insulting comparison)
cards.noteEn: Basura literally means “trash.” In ser una basura de followed by a role, it harshly says that someone is very bad at that role.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links basura to the role being insulted
cards.noteEn: In una basura de followed by a role, de connects the harsh judgment to that role. Natural English normally uses an adjective such as “terrible” instead of translating de.
Mejor compares one option with another. It does not change for gender: una solución mejor and un plan mejor both use mejor.
Adelante can grant permission or challenge someone to continue. It does not literally describe forward movement in this conversational use.
Muestre is the formal command of mostrar, and me is attached because the speaker receives what is shown. The written accent in muéstreme keeps the original stress after me is added.

cards.answerEn: Use the usted command form: regular -ar verbs end in -e, while regular -er and -ir verbs end in -a.
cards.noteEn: Usted is the polite or formal singular “you.” Hablar becomes hable, comer becomes coma, and escribir becomes escriba. Usted is usually left out because the command ending already shows formal address. Some common verbs are irregular, such as decir → diga.
cards.questionEn: How do you politely tell one person to do something in Spanish?

cards.noteEn: With formal usted, su can mean “your.” The same form can also mean “his,” “her,” or “their,” so context identifies the owner.
When propuesta describes a feminine noun, it means “proposed.” As a noun on its own, propuesta can also mean “proposal.”

example.en: We will review the proposed date.

cards.noteEn: Baja is the positive command for one informally addressed person. Te is attached because the verb is bajarse, and the written accent keeps the command's original stress.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone gets off a vehicle or gets down from a surface?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching short word with a form of bajar, then de before the vehicle or surface.
cards.noteEn: The short word changes with the person: me bajo means “I get off,” te bajas means “you get off,” and se baja means “he or she gets off” or “formal you get off.” In a positive informal command, baja and te join as bájate. De introduces what the person leaves.
Bajarse uses de before the vehicle, surface, or place someone leaves. English often translates this de as “off” or “out of.”
Before a noun, maldito can express strong anger or contempt. It is rude or emotionally charged.
Before a full event with its own verb, antes normally begins the connector antes de que.

cards.questionEn: How do you connect one event to a later event that has not happened yet?
cards.answerEn: Use antes de que, then put the pending event's verb in the subjunctive form.
cards.noteEn: The subjunctive is a special verb form used after this connector because the later event has not happened yet. For regular -ar verbs, this form uses an e ending: lanzar becomes lance. If one person performs both actions, Spanish often uses antes de plus the second verb's unchanged dictionary form instead: como antes de salir means “I eat before leaving.”

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of antes de que (“before”)
cards.noteEn: De is a required middle piece when antes introduces a full event with que. Translate antes de que as one connector.

example.en: Let's return before it gets dark.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes antes de que (“before”)
cards.noteEn: Que completes the connector before a full event. The following verb uses a special pending-event form called the subjunctive.

cards.answerEn: I start driving; I start up (subjunctive form)
cards.noteEn: Arranque is a special form of arrancar used for a pending event after a connector such as antes de que. The spelling changes from c to qu so the hard k sound remains before e.

example.es: Avísame antes de que yo arranque.
example.en: Tell me before I start driving.

cards.noteEn: Lance is a special form of lanzar used when the throwing is presented as a pending, wished-for, feared, or otherwise non-asserted event.

example.es: Teme que yo lance la pelota.
example.en: He is afraid that I will throw the ball.

cards.noteEn: Contra can mark the surface or situation that someone or something is thrown or pushed against.

example.es: La ola lanzó la barca contra las rocas.
example.en: The wave threw the boat against the rocks.

cards.noteEn: Cuándo has an accent when it asks, directly or indirectly, at what time something happens.

cards.answerEn: it will change; formal you will change
cards.noteEn: Cambiará keeps the whole dictionary form cambiar and adds -á for the future of one person or thing. Context identifies the subject.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

cards.answerEn: on (before one particular day of the week)
cards.noteEn: Spanish normally uses el before a singular weekday where English uses “on”: el martes means “on Tuesday.” No extra en is needed.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something happens on a particular weekday or regularly on that weekday?
cards.answerEn: Use el before one particular weekday and los before a weekday used for a regular weekly event.
cards.noteEn: Spanish normally uses the article without an extra word for “on”: el martes means “on Tuesday.” The plural article can mark a repeated schedule: los martes means “on Tuesdays.” Weekday names themselves usually stay lowercase in ordinary writing.
